raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by myocardial deposition of misfolded proteins, most commonly immunoglobulin light chain (AL) or transthyretin (ATTR). Amyloid fibrils disrupt extracellular architecture, promote myocardial stiffness, impair longitudinal contraction, and may directly injure myocytes. Although historically considered rare, cardiac amyloidosis is now recognized as an important cause of heart failure, arrhythmia, syncope, aortic stenosis phenocopies, and unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy [1,2].

The clinical phenotype depends on precursor protein. AL amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma-cell disorder and can progress rapidly, with cardiac involvement being the dominant determinant of survival. ATTR amyloidosis results either from age-related deposition of wild-type transthyretin or from pathogenic TTR variants. Comparative cohorts show that AL, hereditary ATTR, and wild-type ATTR differ in age, extracardiac manifestations, biomarker profile, and tempo of decline [3]. The Val122Ile TTR variant is particularly relevant in individuals of African ancestry and is associated with late-onset cardiomyopathy [4]. Autopsy and clinical studies suggest substantial underdiagnosis: wild-type ATTR deposits are common in the very elderly [5], ATTR can be found among patients labelled as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction [6], and concomitant ATTR is increasingly recognized in older patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing valve intervention [7]. In Black patients with cardiac amyloidosis, hereditary ATTR and AL may overlap clinically, making biochemical exclusion of AL essential [8].

Clinical suspicion remains the pivotal first step. Red flags include heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction, increased ventricular wall thickness without longstanding hypertension, low QRS voltage or pseudo-infarct patterns, atrioventricular block, atrial arrhythmias, carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, neuropathy, nephrotic-range proteinuria, macroglossia, periorbital purpura, and intolerance of conventional heart-failure drugs. In suspected AL amyloidosis, serum and urine immunofixation plus serum free light-chain assay are mandatory, because delayed diagnosis may be fatal and monoclonal gammopathy is common in older ATTR patients [9].

Multimodality imaging has transformed diagnosis. Echocardiography typically shows concentric thickening, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling, thickened valves, pericardial effusion, and reduced tissue Doppler velocities. Speckle-tracking strain may demonstrate relative apical sparing, a useful clue in the right clinical context [10]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance adds tissue characterization: native T1 and extracellular volume are elevated [11], and late gadolinium enhancement, often diffuse subendocardial or transmural, has prognostic value [12]. Bone-avid scintigraphy using technetium-labelled tracers was first shown to help distinguish ATTR from AL [13], and pyrophosphate imaging has become widely used in North America [14]. A landmark multicentre study established that grade 2–3 cardiac uptake, in the absence of a monoclonal protein, can diagnose ATTR cardiac amyloidosis non-invasively with very high specificity [15]. If a monoclonal protein is present, or if imaging and clinical data conflict, tissue biopsy with amyloid typing—preferably by mass spectrometry—is required.

Risk stratification guides counselling and treatment urgency. In AL amyloidosis, cardiac troponins and N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide define powerful staging systems [16], later refined by incorporating involved free light-chain burden [17]. In wild-type ATTR, natriuretic peptides, troponin, renal function, and functional class identify clinically meaningful risk strata [18,19]. Serial assessment should integrate symptoms, volume status, biomarkers, renal function, rhythm monitoring, and imaging rather than relying on ventricular ejection fraction alone.

Management has two parallel goals: supportive cardiovascular care and precursor-specific therapy. Diuretics are the mainstay for congestion, often requiring careful titration because stroke volume is fixed and renal perfusion is fragile. Beta-blockers, renin–angiotensin inhibitors, and nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers are frequently poorly tolerated; digoxin is generally avoided or used with extreme caution. Atrial fibrillation is common, and anticoagulation is usually favoured because atrial mechanical dysfunction and intracardiac thrombus may occur even beyond conventional risk scores. Pacemakers are used for conduction disease, whereas primary-prevention defibrillator benefit remains uncertain.

For AL amyloidosis, rapid suppression of the amyloidogenic light chain is the therapeutic emergency. Daratumumab combined with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone has improved haematologic and organ responses in newly diagnosed disease [20]. Selected fit patients may benefit from high-dose melphalan with autologous stem-cell transplantation, while melphalan–dexamethasone remains historically important and illustrates the survival impact of clonal control [21,22].

For ATTR cardiomyopathy, transthyretin stabilization and gene-silencing therapies have changed the outlook. Tafamidis reduced mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in ATTR cardiomyopathy [23], building on earlier stabilization experience in hereditary ATTR neuropathy [24]. Diflunisal can stabilize transthyretin but is limited by renal, gastrointestinal, and fluid-retention toxicity [25]. RNA-targeting therapies such as patisiran and inotersen reduce hepatic transthyretin production and improve hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy, with growing cardiac interest [26,27]. In vivo CRISPR-Cas9 editing has shown proof-of-concept for durable transthyretin reduction, although long-term safety and cardiac outcomes require further study [28]. Contemporary European and American statements emphasize early recognition, rigorous amyloid typing, multidisciplinary care, family screening for hereditary ATTR, and referral to experienced centres when feasible [29,30].
